opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest obstacle is that there's no agreement on what "touch" even is from a data point of view. With cameras, everyone converged on the same thing: a grid of pixels with RGB values. The physics of light is roughly the same no matter whose camera you buy, so an image from one sensor looks a lot like an image from another. That's why we could build huge datasets and pretrained models that transfer.

Tactile sensing is nowhere near that. Some sensors are optical, like the GelSight style, where a camera looks at a deforming gel. Some are capacitive or resistive arrays. Some measure vibration, some measure shear, some just give you a six-axis force-torque reading at the wrist. The resolution, the contact geometry, the materials, and even what physical quantity is measured all differ. So data from one sensor often tells you very little about data from another, and you can't easily pool it.

That leads to a chicken-and-egg problem. Without a standard, nobody collects tactile data at scale, so there's no ImageNet for touch. And without large datasets showing which representations actually help downstream tasks, there's no strong reason for the community or manufacturers to converge on a standard.

There are also practical problems. Tactile sensors wear out, the gels degrade, calibration drifts, and they're hard to mount on many different robot hands. Cameras are cheap, robust, and everywhere because of phones. Touch has no consumer market pushing the cost down and the quality up.

So I'd say the core obstacle is the lack of a shared physical and data abstraction, made worse by the absence of scale. One promising path, rather than waiting for one perfect sensor, is to learn representations that are sensor-agnostic. You'd focus on what touch tells you about the world, like contact location, force, slip, and material properties, instead of the raw signal. If we can map different sensors into that shared space, we might get the benefits of standardization without forcing everyone onto the same hardware.

r001.rationale: The response identifies the lack of agreement on a shared representation and explains that tactile sensors differ in technology, resolution, contact geometry, and measured quantities, making their data hard to combine.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that cameras got lucky in a way that tactile sensors haven't, and probably won't for a while. With a camera, there's a physical fact underneath everything: light hits a sensor, you get a grid of intensities, and the pixel is a pretty universal abstraction. It doesn't matter if it's a phone camera or a Kinect or an industrial sensor, you can resample them into roughly the same thing, and the whole computer vision community can build on top of one representation. That's what let ImageNet happen, that's what let pretraining happen.

Touch doesn't have that. If you look at what's out there right now, you've got optical sensors like GelSight and DIGIT that basically turn touch into an image problem by looking at gel deformation. You've got capacitive arrays, piezoresistive skins, barometric taxels, magnetic sensors, and they're all measuring physically different quantities at different resolutions, different dynamic ranges, different temporal characteristics. Some give you shear, some don't. Some give you vibration, some don't. So the first obstacle is just that there's no agreed-upon physical quantity that "touch" means. Is it a contact patch? A force field? A deformation map? Everyone picks a different answer, and the hardware encodes that choice.

The second thing, which I think people underestimate, is that tactile data is inseparable from the body it's on. An image is more or less meaningful on its own. A tactile reading only makes sense relative to the geometry of the finger, the compliance of the skin, where it's mounted, what the robot was doing at that moment. So even if two labs used the same sensor, the data from a parallel-jaw gripper and a five-fingered hand looks completely different in distribution. That makes it really hard to pool data the way vision did.

And then there's the boring but real issue: scale and durability. Cameras are a commodity, you can buy millions of them, they don't wear out. Tactile sensors are mostly research artifacts, they degrade, the gel tears, calibration drifts. So you never get the dataset size that forces a standard to emerge from sheer gravity.

My own take is that the standard probably won't come from the hardware converging. It's more likely to come from the learning side, where you have models that take heterogeneous tactile inputs and learn a shared latent representation, something closer to how we handle multimodal data generally. The "pixel" of touch might end up being learned rather than designed. But that only works once there's enough data across enough sensors to learn it, and we're still early on that.

r001.rationale: The response calls the lack of an agreed physical quantity for touch the “first obstacle” and explains that tactile sensor types measure different quantities with different resolutions and capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest obstacle is that tactile sensing is so tightly coupled to the hardware. With cameras, you have a fairly consistent interface: an image is a grid of pixels. With touch, different sensors might measure pressure, deformation, or shear, and their signals depend on the material, the geometry, and how the sensor is mounted on the robot.

So the challenge is figuring out what the shared representation should preserve. Is it contact force? Is it the geometry of the contact? Is it whether something is slipping? Those are related, but they’re not interchangeable. And touch is also active—what you feel depends on how you move and interact with the object.

I think we need more data across different sensors and embodiments, tied to actual manipulation tasks, before we can tell which parts of the representation should be universal and which need to stay specific to the hardware.

r001.rationale: The response identifies tactile sensing’s dependence on hardware and the differing signals measured by different sensors as the main obstacle to a shared representation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest obstacle is that tactile sensors don’t all measure the same thing in the same way. With cameras, you have a fairly consistent representation: a grid of pixels measuring light. With touch, one sensor might measure pressure, another deformation, another shear force. And the signal depends on the sensor’s material, its geometry, where it’s mounted, and how you make contact.

So the question is, what should we standardize? The raw sensor output, or the physical information we want to infer—like contact location, force, or whether something is slipping? I think we need a useful shared representation at that second level, while allowing different sensor designs underneath. But getting there requires data across sensors and tasks, so we can figure out what actually transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says tactile sensors measure different things in different ways and identifies this as the biggest obstacle to a shared representation comparable to cameras.
